deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivation. It is part of Riemann's notebook of excerpts from Herbart (bundle 'Naturphilosophie'). It continues from the previous page, which quotes Herbart's 1796 notes on Schelling's 'Vom Ich' (Werke XII, 35 ff.).

(1) Top lines. These end the Schelling excerpt: '...darum folgen müsse, sehe ich nicht ein.' Then a remark: on Fichte's (or Schelling's) premises, if consistent, time and change can be posited only as not real, never as real.

(2) Heading '(Abstraction)', then the excerpt 'XII. 55'. This is Herbart's early (c. 1797–98) argument on the 'Intension' (intensive magnitude) of the Ich. Reconstructed as an argument about magnitudes:
- The concept of the Ich requires that the act of positing (Setzen) be separated from what is posited (Gesetztes), since the latter is contingent.
- Every actual positing comes bound to something posited. To abstract the bare act, the general concept of positing, one must think the positing in an infinitely higher degree than the posited.
- In any single actual positing, the positing cannot exceed the posited in degree.
- So this 'infinite preponderance' must be accumulated from many different positings that share only the act.
- Hence the rational being reaches the general concept of positing only by thinking infinitely many positings, with the posited contents in infinitely smaller degrees.

In modern shorthand, mine and only illustrative: if each positing i has act-strength a_i and content-strength c_i with a_i ≈ c_i, the abstract act is a limit in which the act-component dominates. The common act aggregates while the heterogeneous contents average out, so the ratio act : content tends to infinity.

Herbart concludes this is the 'strict proof' that the activity of the Ich must be thought as an intension consisting of innumerable (unzählbare) degrees.

(3) Consequence. The positing keeps enough intension, but the posited cannot come about. That is the origin of striving or willing (Streben, Wollen). A positing that strives toward greater intension is positing and striving at once. When the present feeling is reinforced by long duration, the relative intension of the first diminishes.

(4) 'XII. 57'. The thesis is: 'the intension of willing depends on the strength of the preceding actual positing relative to the present one'. Herbart's commentary:
- The first positing is converted only partly into striving.
- A strong positing can yield a strong striving because there is much to inhibit.
- If the inhibiting factor is weak, the striving is weak, but the actual representation stays livelier. Such a weak striving can still express itself strongly as desire, since nothing counterbalances it.
- There is then an obscure discussion of an 'acceleration' (Beschleunigung) that duration should impart to positing. Herbart concludes it is largely an acceleration of a striving rather than of a positing.

The quantities here are qualitative (stronger/weaker, ratio, growth with duration). No equations are written.

(5) In red ink: 'Anmerk. 1.' to Herbart's 1822 essay 'Über die Möglichkeit und Nothwendigkeit, Mathematik auf Psychologie anzuwenden' (Werke VII, 153). This is Herbart's autobiographical account:
- Fichte made the Ich (the conditions of self-consciousness) a problem.
- Herbart first saw that the Ich is the most dependent and conditioned thing, not primitive.
- Second, he saw that the original representations must be partly opposed and so inhibit one another. Inhibited representations are not lost but persist as strivings, which return to actual consciousness when the inhibition is lifted.
- 'This inhibition could and had to be calculated', so psychology needs a mathematical as well as a metaphysical foundation.

The page serves as Riemann's documentation of the genesis of Herbart's mathematical psychology: intensive degrees, inhibition, striving. This bears on Riemann's own natural-philosophical fragments, where Herbart is a known influence.
errors: There is no computation to check. Herbart's 'strict proof' is a conceptual argument; its passage from 'many positings sharing only the act' to an 'infinite' preponderance of act over content (an actual infinity of degrees) is not justified, only asserted.
The XII.57 discussion of 'Beschleunigung' is internally obscure. As transcribed it does not yield a definite quantitative law.

results.what: Herbart's argument that the activity of the Ich is an intensive magnitude made of innumerably many degrees (Werke XII, 55)
results.modern_name: Herbartian intensive-magnitude theory of mental acts (precursor of psychophysical quantification)
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Herbart (c. 1797–98, published posthumously in Werke XII)

results.what: Intension of willing proportional to the strength of the earlier actual positing relative to the present one; inhibited positing becomes striving
results.modern_name: Herbart's theory of inhibition (Hemmung) and striving (Streben)

results.what: Programmatic claim that inhibition of representations can and must be calculated, so psychology needs a mathematical foundation
results.modern_name: Herbart's mathematical psychology (Psychologie als Wissenschaft 1824–25; 1822 essay)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a verbatim excerpt notebook of Herbart's texts (Werke XII and VII), with no original mathematics by Riemann. Riemann's close study of Herbart's psychology and metaphysics is well documented (Scholz, Ferreirós and others).
transcription_corrections: Line 2: in 'Zeit und Wechsel zwar als [wirklich] nicht wirklich', the first 'wirklich' is struck through. Read 'zwar als nicht wirklich, niemals aber als wirklich gesetzt werden können'.
'(Abstraction)' is an underlined heading centered above XII. 55, not part of the running text.
'wenn es nicht [?] sein soll': the illegible word is possibly 'leer' (uncertain).
'(s. die [?] Vorarbeiten)': possibly '(s. die Kantischen Vorarbeiten)' (uncertain).
'das Ich nicht als ein Factum[?] in sich schließen können': the image suggests possibly 'als ein Fertiges' rather than 'Factum' (uncertain).
'Demnach leidet jene Beschleunigung nichts und vermehren[?] die schon gestärkten Intension...' is more plausibly 'und vermehrt nur die schon gestärkte Intension des ersten...' (uncertain).
The final 'Anmerk. 1. zu ...' paragraph is written in red ink, marking a separate excerpt from Herbart Werke VII, 153. There is a footnote mark '1)' at the right margin.
